newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's property market soars as China rule looms.
newsitem.headline: HK's property market soars as China rule looms.

text.p: The thunder of pile-drivers across Hong Kong from morning to night is a clear testament of the booming state of the British colony's property market.
Soaring real estate prices have created a generation of millionaires in Hong Kong, if their wealth is judged by the value of their homes.
Sometimes, not even a pocket-sized plot of land seems safe from the developers in this territory of just 1,067 square km (412 square miles).
"People have tended to make more money out of buying and owning property than working in a job," said Martin Tacon, a property analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston.

The change of sovereignty from British to Chinese rule in only 100 days -- at midnight on June 30 -- is not expected to slow the frenzy that pushed residential property prices up some 20 to 30 percent in 1996.

Prices gained a further five to 10 percent during the first few months of this year and expectations of a smooth transition should underpin 15 to 20 percent growth in residential prices for the whole of 1997, experts say.
Over recent months, a typical weekend for a Hong Kong family could consist of joining a queue of thousands of people lining up to view tiny new apartments being offered for sale.
"It's a bit of a national pastime," said Tacon.
Buyers can make millions in a matter of months and even the rights to buy a property, for which people also queue for hours, have reportedly fetched up to HK$2 million.
"It is definitely a vote of confidence," said one analyst.

Despite the frenetic pace of construction in Hong Kong, there is an acute shortage of supply. The race to erect residential and office towers has failed to keep up with the growing population, which stood at 6.42 million in 1996.
Hong Kong saw a net inflow of 118,500 people last year.
"People are returning that have previously emigrated," said Pauline Gately, regional strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"It is a reflection of Hong Kong's vibrancy," she said.
The bloody 1989 crackdown on the pro-democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square shook confidence in the territory, leading to an outflow of people seeking residency elsewhere.
"They therefore have a safe haven taken care of and they want to come back here and make money," said Marshall Mays, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center.
The handover is expected to spur further economic integration, bringing more business opportunities and liquidity flows from the mainland.

"Positive sentiment generated by the handover will underpin short-term activities. In the longer term, stronger economic growth in both Hong Kong and China will stimulate demand for property in the territory," said real estate consultancy Jones Lang Wootton in its Asia Pacific Property report for 1997.

James Liu, a Taiwan-born Chinese, is one of the many who recognised the thriving business opportunities in Hong Kong. He moved here in 1994 from Canada and runs a luxury beauty company. He expects business as usual after the handover.
"Asia is a really happening place," he said.
Liu has bought and sold property three times in two years.
His first apartment, a 500 sq ft (56-1/2 sq metres) flat in the busy Causeway Bay shopping district, cost him HK$2 million.
He sold that in August 1996 for almost HK$2.8 million and bought another property for HK$1.85 million. "That was a good deal and was sold for about HK$2.5 million," said Liu.
Only a month ago Liu closed a HK$3.5 million deal on a 700 sq ft (65 sq metres) flat in a residential area on Hong Kong island.
The apartment in the Mid-Levels area gives him a scenic view of Hong Kong's Central district skyscrapers and Victoria Harbour.
"Property, if you buy it right, is probably the quickest way to make money," he said.
